# INTRODUCTION

This chapter identifies the problem that the study addresses and defines the objectives of a solution. It describes why the problem matters, what the study asks and aims to achieve, the frameworks behind the study, and the boundaries and significance of the study.

## Introduction to the Study

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone], about eight or nine tropical cyclones cross the Philippines each year. During these events, Filipinos use social media to warn others, report damage, and ask for help [@ermino2022urgency; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Natural language processing (NLP) can help responders find the useful information in these posts [@lewis2025tapping]. Two NLP tasks are the subject of this study. Humanitarian classification assigns each post a category by the type of report [@alam2021humaid], and named entity recognition (NER) identifies details such as affected locations and requests for aid [@ali2026humaidner].

A single model can be trained on both tasks, and such a model is called a multi-task model. Learning one task may help the model learn the other [@wang2021transformer], but it may also interfere with it, a problem known as negative transfer [@royer2023scalarization]. Multi-task optimizers are algorithms meant to reduce this problem by balancing how the tasks influence the model during training [@xin2022mtohelp]. Taglish, the mixing of Tagalog and English in the same text, is widespread in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. None of the studies reviewed has compared these optimizers on Taglish posts.

This study builds a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both tasks and trains a multi-task model on it. It compares 13 multi-task optimizers in negative transfer and training cost, selects one of them for the final multi-task model, and compares the final multi-task model with single-task models. The study contributes the dataset, the final multi-task model, and evidence on how much these optimizers reduce negative transfer and at what training cost.

## Background of the Study

The Philippines faces the highest disaster risk among 193 countries, partly because of its high exposure to weather-related extremes [@bundnis2025worldriskreport]. During disasters, social media posts provide responders with firsthand information from affected communities, but the large number of posts makes it time-consuming to find actionable details [@somido2023actionable]. Researchers have turned to NLP to automate this process by classifying posts and extracting key information [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot].

Several Philippine studies have applied NLP to disaster posts. For classification, @ermino2022urgency categorized typhoon posts by urgency, and @somido2023actionable identified informative disaster posts. For extraction, @yute2021satellite applied NER to extract location names from posts about the 2020 Taal Volcano eruption. More recently, @caoile2025urdaneta used a large language model (LLM) to extract place names and detect sentiment, urgency, and intent in Facebook comments. However, each of these studies either trained a model for a single task or relied on an LLM instead of a trained model.

A multi-task model could provide both kinds of information at the same time. It shares one pretrained transformer encoder between the tasks and gives each task its own task head, the part of the model that makes the predictions for that task [@wang2021transformer; @gama2026uniform]. Because the encoder has already learned general patterns of language during pretraining, it can be fine-tuned, or trained further, on a relatively small dataset annotated for both tasks [@bucher2024finetuned].

However, a multi-task model can show negative transfer and perform worse on a task than a single-task model [@kurin2022unitary; @royer2023scalarization]. This drop in performance has been reported when classification and NER are trained together. In @zhu2025prefinetuning, an encoder trained on both tasks performed slightly worse than single-task baselines because the two tasks made conflicting demands on the encoder. Similarly, @ali2026humaidner found that classification performance declined during joint training. The authors attributed the decline to an imbalance, because NER provides a training signal for every token and classification provides only one for the whole post.

Multi-task optimizers differ in how they balance the tasks. Equal weighting keeps the weights of both tasks the same throughout training, and specialized multi-task optimizers (SMTOs) adjust how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds [@gama2026uniform]. Studies disagree on whether SMTOs reduce negative transfer better than equal weighting. When evaluated against equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] or well-tuned fixed weights [@xin2022mtohelp], SMTOs often showed no performance advantage, despite the extra training time and memory that many of them need. In contrast, @gama2026uniform found that SMTOs matched equal weighting on two similar tasks but outperformed it on more complex problems.

These studies leave two research gaps. First, none of the studies reviewed provides Taglish posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. Evaluating both outputs of a multi-task model requires posts annotated for both tasks. While @ali2026humaidner built such a dataset for English by adding NER spans to existing HumAID posts [@alam2021humaid], Tagalog and Taglish still have few annotated datasets [@cruz2022tagalog; @herrera2022tweettaglish]. Second, none of the studies reviewed compares multi-task optimizers for humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish posts, in either negative transfer or training cost. Because the performance of multi-task optimizers depends on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the optimizer that best reduces negative transfer cannot be known in advance and must be found by comparing the optimizers on these posts.

## Statement of the Problem

During a tropical cyclone, responders cannot easily find useful information among the large number of Taglish posts. A multi-task model could label each post with its humanitarian category and its entities at the same time, but two things are missing. First, none of the studies reviewed provides Taglish posts annotated for both tasks, so such a model can be neither trained nor evaluated. Second, none of them compares multi-task optimizers on these two tasks for Taglish posts, so it is not known which optimizer best reduces negative transfer or at what training cost. The study addresses this problem by answering four research questions.

1. What F1-scores do single-task models achieve for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts? (Baseline Analysis)

2. How can a dataset and a multi-task model be designed for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts? (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. How do the 13 multi-task optimizers compare in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory? (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. How does the final multi-task model compare with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory? (Comparative Validation)

## Objectives

The general objective is to develop a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to compare multi-task optimizers for this model in negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, the study pursues four objectives.

1. To measure the F1-scores of single-task models for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts. (Baseline Analysis)

2. To design and build a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts. (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. To compare the 13 multi-task optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory. (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. To compare the final multi-task model with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory. (Comparative Validation)

## Hypotheses

The study tests the following null and alternative hypotheses for each of the two tasks, humanitarian classification and NER.

**Null hypothesis ($H_0$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model is the same as that of the single-task model for that task.

**Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model differs from that of the single-task model for that task.

## Theoretical Framework

This study is grounded in the theory of multi-task learning of Caruana [-@caruana1997multitask]. Under this theory, a model that learns related tasks together shares what it learns among them, so that learning one task can help the others. This effect is called inductive transfer. Positive transfer occurs when learning the tasks together improves performance on a task, and negative transfer occurs when learning one task interferes with learning the other [@royer2023scalarization]. Multi-task models performed better than single-task models in some studies [@wang2021transformer] and worse in others [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. In this study, the two tasks share a pretrained transformer encoder, so the final multi-task model may show either positive or negative transfer on each task. The hypotheses therefore test for a difference in F1-score in either direction.

## Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework of this study consists of the research paradigm in @fig-research-paradigm and the design of the multi-task model in @fig-artifact. It centers on two comparisons, one among the 13 multi-task optimizers and one between the final multi-task model and the single-task models.

![Research Paradigm](figures/fig-1-1-research-paradigm.pdf){#fig-research-paradigm}

@fig-research-paradigm follows the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model. The inputs are the Taglish posts, the humanitarian categories of HumAID, the entity types of HUMAID-NER, the pretrained transformer encoder, the 13 multi-task optimizers, and the laptop used for training. The process has four steps, each answering one research question. First, the dataset and the multi-task model are designed and built (RQ2). Second, a single-task model is trained for each task to measure the baseline F1-scores (RQ1). Third, the 13 multi-task optimizers are compared, and the optimizer of the final multi-task model is selected based on negative transfer (RQ3). Fourth, the final multi-task model is compared with the single-task models (RQ4). The outputs are the dataset, the final multi-task model, and the comparison of the 13 multi-task optimizers.

![Multi-Task Model](figures/fig-1-2-artifact.pdf){#fig-artifact}

@fig-artifact shows how the multi-task model processes an example post. One pretrained transformer encoder is shared by both tasks and reads the post once. The classification head uses the output for the whole post to assign a humanitarian category, and the NER head uses the output for each token to mark the entities. The dashed lines show the steps that occur only during training. Each head produces a loss, which measures how far its predictions are from the correct labels. The multi-task optimizer uses the two losses to update the shared encoder so that the model improves on both tasks.

## Scope, Limitations, and Delimitations

### Scope of the Study

The study builds a dataset of about 2,500 Taglish posts on X, formerly Twitter, about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. The posts were written from one day before each tropical cyclone entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility to three days after it left, based on the dates in the preliminary reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. The Philippine Area of Responsibility is the area that PAGASA monitors for tropical cyclones. Each post is annotated with one of the 10 humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] and with entity spans of the 10 entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

Two single-task models are trained on the dataset, one for each task, together with a multi-task model that performs both tasks. All models use the same pretrained transformer encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was pretrained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The multi-task model is trained with each of the 13 multi-task optimizers reviewed in Section 2.2. This gives 13 candidate multi-task models, and the final multi-task model is selected from them based on negative transfer.

The study measures the agreement between the annotators on the humanitarian categories. For every model, it measures the F1-score on each task, the training time, and the peak memory. The final multi-task model is then used in a prototype web application that labels a stream of test posts and shows them on a map and in a table, and each feature of the prototype is checked with functional tests.

### Limitations of the Study

The dataset does not represent all Taglish posts about tropical cyclones. The posts come only from users of X, who may not represent everyone affected by tropical cyclones. X also does not reliably show the region of a user, so the Taglish of some regions may be rare or missing. The keywords cover only the roots *bagyo* and *baha* and the words formed from them. A post about a tropical cyclone that uses neither root is not in the dataset. Examples are a request for rescue that mentions only submerged houses and a post that gives only the name of the storm. Posts that mention a tropical cyclone or flooding in these words may therefore be overrepresented, and humanitarian categories whose posts rarely use them may have few posts. Posts written outside the collection windows are also left out. A post counts as Taglish when a dictionary finds at least one English word and at least one Tagalog word in it (Section 3.3). Some posts in the dataset may therefore be almost entirely in one language, and the dictionary may assign some words to the wrong language. The threshold of 0.75 for duplicates was set on posts that were mostly in English [@alam2021crisisbench] and is not checked again on Taglish posts, so some near duplicates may remain and some distinct posts may be removed. Only the post IDs are shared, and posts deleted on X are removed, so other researchers may later be unable to retrieve the whole dataset.

The dataset is small. Its size of about 2,500 posts is set by how much two annotators can finish, not by what the models need, and the learning curve checks whether it is enough (Section 3.7). The dataset may have even fewer posts when too few eligible posts are found (Section 3.5). The test set is about 350 posts, so every F1-score on it is estimated from a small number of posts. The posts are not expected to be spread evenly over the 10 humanitarian categories, and no class weights or oversampling are used in training (Section 3.5). The models may therefore perform poorly on rare categories, and a rare category may have too few test posts for a precise F1-score. A category with too few posts to appear in the training, validation, and test sets is left out of macro-F1 (Section 3.3).

The humanitarian categories are assigned by two members of the research group, who are not trained in disaster response. Each post is given exactly one category even when it fits more than one, so part of the information in such posts is not recorded. Annotation of the sample begins after at most three practice batches, even when Cohen's kappa is still below .61, and a batch whose kappa falls below .61 is not annotated again (Section 3.5). Disagreements that the annotators cannot settle are decided by a single adjudicator, and these decisions are not checked by anyone else.

The entity spans are marked automatically by GLiNER and are not checked by a person (Section 3.5). GLiNER is not trained on the posts of the study, and how often it is correct on Taglish posts is not measured, so the number of errors in the spans is unknown. The models that perform NER learn from these spans and are also scored against them. The F1-scores for NER therefore show how well a model reproduces the output of GLiNER, not how well it finds the entities that a person would mark.

The training setup is limited by the laptop. The embedding layer of the encoder is not trained and the batch size is 8, so that every optimizer fits in 8 GB of GPU memory (Section 3.5). The F1-scores may be lower than they would be on a computer with more memory. Only the learning rate is tuned for each model, over four values and with one run for each value. The other settings of the optimizers are kept at the values in Appendix C, and an optimizer might perform better with settings tuned for it. Linear scalarization is the exception. Its task weights are tuned as well, so it receives more tuning runs than the other optimizers. The training time and peak memory are measured on one laptop and may differ on other computers.

The comparisons rest on few runs. Each model is trained only five times, so the comparison of the 13 optimizers is descriptive, and small differences between them may come from the random seeds and not from the optimizers. The candidate multi-task models are compared on the validation set, which is also used to tune the learning rate and to choose the best epoch of each run. Their validation scores are therefore likely to be higher than their scores on new posts. The final multi-task model is selected by the average of its relative changes on the two tasks, so it may still show negative transfer on one of them. With only five pairs of runs, the paired t-tests may fail to detect a small difference between the final multi-task model and a single-task model, and the normality of the differences that the test assumes cannot be verified. The error analysis examines one run of the final multi-task model, and its findings may not hold for the other runs.

The findings may not hold beyond this study. The posts are about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026, and the findings may not generalize to other years. The optimizers are compared on one pair of tasks and one pretrained transformer encoder. Because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the best optimizer may differ for other tasks or encoders. The study uses the categories and entity types of HUMAID-NER, but that dataset is in English, is much larger, and has a similar number of posts in each category [@ali2026humaidner]. The F1-scores of the two studies can therefore be compared only loosely.

### Delimitations of the Study

The posts are collected only from X. X allows posts collected through its API to be stored, provided that posts deleted on the platform are also removed [@x2026devpolicy], and earlier disaster datasets also rely on posts from this platform [@ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @alam2021humaid]. Other Philippine languages, such as Cebuano and Waray, are left out, because mixing languages would make it unclear whether the model performs equally well in each language. Natural hazards other than tropical cyclones, such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, are also left out. Tropical cyclones alone give several events within a single year, because about eight or nine of them cross the Philippines each year [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone]. Earlier years are left out because one year already has far more matching posts than the two annotators can annotate, and the study does not examine how language changes over time. December 2026 is left out because collection must end before annotation begins that month. Images, video, and audio are left out because both tasks work on text.

The model performs only humanitarian classification and NER. Other tasks, such as sentiment analysis, urgency detection, and hazard classification, are left out because each added task would change how the tasks interfere with one another, and differences in negative transfer would be harder to attribute to the optimizers. The model therefore does not rate the urgency of a post or identify the type of hazard. It does not translate posts into English, because the encoder was pretrained on both English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. It does not check whether a post is true, because that requires outside sources such as official reports.

The comparison covers existing multi-task optimizers, and no new optimizer is developed. Optimizers other than the 13 are left out because they do not meet the two selection criteria in Section 3.2. Other encoders are left out so that the optimizer remains the only difference among the candidate multi-task models. Other computers are left out so that the training time and peak memory of every model are measured under the same conditions. The final multi-task model and the single-task models are tested only on the test set of this study. They are not tested on HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], which is in English and whose entity spans were annotated with a different method. The final multi-task model is also not compared with LLMs, such as GPT, which differ in size, training, and deployment cost. Earlier studies have already made this comparison for text classification [@bucher2024finetuned], including disaster posts [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot].

The prototype only demonstrates the final multi-task model. It is not deployed or used during an actual disaster, and its usability is not evaluated with the staff of local disaster risk reduction and management offices, because the objectives of the study are to build the dataset and the model, to compare the optimizers, and to compare the final multi-task model with the single-task models. How correctly the prototype places posts on the map is also not evaluated, because the place list is not part of the final multi-task model. The software is not maintained after the study. The final multi-task model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset are instead published on GitHub, so that other researchers can retrain and adapt the model for new events.

## Significance of the Study

This study mainly benefits researchers in NLP and in crisis informatics, the field that examines how social media information can support disaster response. These researchers gain a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER, which none of the studies reviewed provides, to train and evaluate models for both tasks.

For researchers in multi-task learning, the study provides evidence on how well SMTOs reduce negative transfer compared with equal weighting, and at what training cost. Because studies disagree on whether SMTOs perform better [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @gama2026uniform], these findings add evidence from posts that mix two languages and have few annotated resources.

For local disaster risk reduction and management offices, the study shows, as a proof of concept, how one multi-task model can classify incoming posts and extract their entities at the same time. The comparison with the single-task models shows what is gained and lost by using one multi-task model in place of two single-task models. The prototype shows how responders could find requests for rescue and relief more quickly during a disaster.

Future researchers can extend this work through the public release of the final multi-task model, source code, annotation guidelines, and dataset post IDs on GitHub. With these, others can retrain the model on future tropical cyclones, build similar datasets for other Philippine languages, or integrate additional disaster response tasks such as urgency detection.

## Definitions of Terms

**Annotation:** The process of marking text with descriptive information to produce a dataset for machine learning, or the information that results. In this study, two annotators assign the humanitarian categories to the posts in doccano, and GLiNER marks the entity spans.

**Candidate multi-task model:** One of the 13 multi-task models, each trained with a different multi-task optimizer. The final multi-task model is selected from them.

**Equal weighting:** The multi-task optimizer that adds the losses of the tasks with the same weight throughout training [@kurin2022unitary]. In this study, the training cost of the other 12 optimizers is measured against it.

**F1-score:** A score from 0 to 1 that combines precision and recall. Precision is the proportion of the predictions of a model that are correct, and recall is the proportion of the annotated items that the model finds. In this study, humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of the F1-scores of the categories. NER is scored with span-level micro-F1, which counts an entity as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match the annotation [@ali2026humaidner].

**Final multi-task model:** The candidate multi-task model that is selected from the 13 based on negative transfer. It is compared with the single-task models and used in the prototype web application.

**Humanitarian classification:** The task of assigning a post one category that names the kind of humanitarian information it reports [@alam2021humaid]. In this study, each post receives one of the 10 categories of HumAID, such as requests or urgent needs.

**Inter-annotator agreement:** How often annotators who work independently give the same item the same label. In this study, it is measured with Cohen's kappa between the two annotators on the humanitarian categories [@cohen1960coefficient].

**Label:** A class, category, or tag assigned to text, or the process of assigning one. In this study, the labels are the 10 humanitarian categories and the 10 entity types, and labeling refers to a model assigning them to posts, such as the final multi-task model labeling incoming posts in the prototype.

**Loss:** A measure of how far the predictions of a model are from the correct labels. Training reduces the loss. In this study, each task has its own cross-entropy loss.

**Multi-task model:** A model that is trained on several tasks together, with part of the model shared by all the tasks [@caruana1997multitask]. In this study, it is one pretrained transformer encoder shared by a task head for humanitarian classification and a task head for NER.

**Multi-task optimizer:** An algorithm that decides how the losses of the tasks are used together to update a multi-task model during training [@lin2023libmtl]. In this study, 13 multi-task optimizers are compared.

**Named entity recognition (NER):** The task of finding the words or phrases in a text that name specific details and assigning each an entity type. In this study, the posts are annotated with the 10 entity types of HUMAID-NER, such as locations and requests [@ali2026humaidner].

**Negative transfer:** A drop in performance on a task when it is trained together with another task, compared with training it alone [@royer2023scalarization]. In this study, it is a lower F1-score of a candidate multi-task model on a task than that of the single-task model for that task, and a higher F1-score is positive transfer.

**Peak memory:** The largest amount of GPU memory allocated during one training run.

**Post:** A message published on social media. In this study, it is a public post on X, which the title calls a Tweet, the name used when X was called Twitter.

**Pretrained transformer encoder:** A language model that is trained on large amounts of text before it is used for a task. It turns the tokens of a text into numbers that the task heads use. In this study, it is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was pretrained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

**Single-task model:** A model trained on one task only. In this study, each single-task model uses the same pretrained transformer encoder as the multi-task model with one task head, and its F1-score is the baseline for measuring negative transfer on that task.

**Specialized multi-task optimizer (SMTO):** A multi-task optimizer that adjusts how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds [@gama2026uniform]. In this study, these are the 11 of the 13 optimizers that do not keep the task weights fixed.

**Taglish:** The mixing of Tagalog and English in the same text, also called code-switching [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. In this study, a post is Taglish when it has at least one English word and one Tagalog word.

**Task head:** The part of a multi-task or single-task model that makes the predictions for one task from the output of the pretrained transformer encoder.

**Token:** A word or part of a word that the pretrained transformer encoder reads as one unit.

**Training cost:** The training time and peak memory of a model. Training time is the time that one run spends on training steps.

**Typhoon:** Used in the title for any tropical cyclone, which is a rotating storm that forms over warm ocean water. In this study, it covers all tropical cyclones that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility from January to November 2026.
